item.title: Psychological distress, perceived psychological reward, and nicotine dependence among young people
item.description:
Background: E-cigarettes (ECs) remain the most commonly used tobacco product among young people in the United States (US). Psychological distress (PD) is prevalent and associated with EC use and nicotine dependence, although underlying factors are unclear. Psychological reward (PR)-positive internal sensations associated with EC use-may account for the association between PD and nicotine dependence. This study examined whether PR was statistically associated with the relationship between PD and nicotine dependence. Given the cross-sectional design, analyses assessed associations rather than causal or temporal pathways.

Methods: Young people aged 14-25 years in the US who had recently initiated EC use participated in a study of nicotine product trajectories. After providing consent or assent, participants completed an online survey. Measures included PD (anxiety and depression symptoms), PR (feeling calm, less irritable, better able to concentrate, more awake, and less hungry after EC use), and nicotine dependence (Hooked on Nicotine Checklist). The indirect association between PD and nicotine dependence through PR was examined using linear regression.

Results: The direct association between PD and nicotine dependence remained significant (b = 0.22), as did the estimated indirect association through PR (b = 0.06, 95% CI [0.01, 0.10]).

Conclusion: Findings indicate cross-sectional associations among PD, PR of EC use, and nicotine dependence in young people. Addressing PD may be relevant to efforts to reduce nicotine dependence; longitudinal and experimental studies are needed to determine whether PD management influences dependence.

Figueroa W, Ferketich AK, Breitborde N, Patterson JG, Tackett AP, Lu B

item.title: Daily polysubstance use associated with HIV, HCV, and non-fatal overdose among people who inject drugs: A latent class analysis using nationwide data
item.description:
Background: This study examined how distinct patterns of polysubstance use are associated with non-fatal overdose, human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection, and lifetime hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection among persons who inject drugs (PWID).

Methods: PWID were recruited from 23 U.S. cities for the 2018 National HIV Behavioral Surveillance. Latent class analysis was conducted using eight daily substance use indicators, including cannabis, opioid injection, cocaine-crack injection, methamphetamine injection, opioid non-injection, cocaine-crack non-injection, methamphetamine non-injection, and benzodiazepine non-injection. Associations between latent classes and sociodemographic variables, behavioral risk factors and non-fatal overdose, HIV infection, and lifetime HCV were analyzed using the R3STEP and Vermunt's 3-Step procedure.

Results: In total, 11,347 PWID were included in the analysis. Four classes were determined: 1) Opioid-Only Injection (46.79%), 2) Polydrug-Polyroute (4.07%), 3) Cocaine Dominant Polyroute OSPU (35.96%), and 4) Meth Dominant Polyroute OSPU (13.18%). After adjusting for covariates (e.g., sociodemographic, psychological distress, sexual and physical violence, attending drug treatment in the past 12 months), the Opioid-Only Injection class had a higher proportion of PWID who tested positive for HIV than all polysubstance classes and higher lifetime HCV than the Polydrug-Polyroute and Cocaine Dominant Polyroute OSPU classes. The polysubstance use classes had higher proportions of non-fatal overdose than the Opioid-Only Injection class, and the Polydrug-Polyroute class had greater non-fatal overdose episodes than all other classes.

Discussion: This study identified four novel polysubstance-polyroute typologies and their unique relationships with non-fatal overdose, HIV, and HCV risk among a nationwide sample of PWID. Interventions to mitigate infectious disease and non-fatal overdose risk among PWID may benefit from tailoring responses based on the needs of specific drug use combinations that individuals use daily.

item.title: Coping patterns moderate the association between negative affect and potential proxies for hypersexual behavior in stimulant-using men who have sex with men
item.description:
Background: Stimulant-using men who have sex with men (MSM) experience mental and sexual health challenges, which may be partially influenced by individual coping patterns (i.e., problem-focused, emotion-focused, dysfunctional). In the current analysis, we examined the frequency of certain coping patterns as a moderator of the association between negative affect and hypersexual behavior among stimulant-using MSM METHODS: Baseline data from a sample of MSM who participated in a randomized control trial focused on stimulant use and sex were analyzed. Multiple regression models examined associations between negative affect and two proxies of hypersexuality (controlling for stimulant-use frequency): (1) sexual compulsivity and (2) meeting diagnostic criteria for a proposed DSM-5 hypersexual disorder. Patterns of coping moderators were also evaluated across regression models.

Results: A total of 206 MSM were included in this analysis, with most identifying as gay and as non-Hispanic/Latino White. They had a mean age of 39.6 years. Negative affect was significantly associated with sexual compulsivity (B=0.40, p < 0.001) and with positive screening for the proposed DSM-5 hypersexual disorder (RR=1.93, p < 0.01). Problem-focused and emotion-focused coping patterns significantly moderate the relations between negative affect and sexual compulsivity, such that higher frequency of these coping patterns buffered the association between negative affect and sexual compulsivity, while lower frequency did not. There was no significant moderation of dysfunctional coping patterns on either hypersexuality outcome.

Discussion: Negative affect and problem-focused and emotion-focused coping patterns may be important variables influencing hypersexual behavior among stimulant-using MSM, with each potentially being modifiable in terms of cognitive and behavioral intervention approaches.

Weinstein ER, Carino KR, Tishler E, Pantalone DW, Biello KB, Mayer KH

item.title: Cannabis retail accessibility and adolescent use across a maturing market: Evidence from Canada
item.description:
Introduction: The rapid expansion of commercial cannabis retail following legalization in Canada has raised concerns about adolescent cannabis use. This study examined whether spatial accessibility to cannabis retailers was associated with cannabis use among secondary school students.

Methods: Repeat cross-sectional data were drawn from the COMPASS study (2018-2023), including 419,887 students across Alberta, British Columbia, Ontario, and Quebec. Student survey data were linked with geospatial measures of cannabis retail accessibility, including distance to nearest retailer, retailer density, and inverse distance weighted density within 2000 m of schools. Multilevel logistic regression models examined associations with ever use, past 12-month use, past 30-day use, and daily/almost daily use. Multilevel ordinal regression assessed use frequency among users. Models adjusted for individual- and school-level covariates, with clustering at the school level.

Results: Cannabis use declined over time, with past 12-month use decreasing from 22.2% in 2018-10.0% in 2023. Associations between spatial accessibility measures and cannabis use outcomes were generally small, inconsistent, and often non-significant. Sensitivity analyses across 264 model specifications supported null effects. Among students who reported cannabis, greater geographic accessibility was associated with higher use frequency in 2018, but this relationship disappeared as retail availability expanded. Perceived ease of access was strongly associated with cannabis use but modestly correlated with retail accessibility.

Conclusions: Spatial accessibility to cannabis retailers was associated with more frequent adolescent cannabis use early in the post-legalization period, but this relationship weakened as retail outlets became widespread. Policies focused on retailer proximity may have limited impact in mature retail markets.

Seabrook JA, Zhong S, Cole AG, Philipneri A, Anderson KK, Barakat C

item.title: PrEP stigma and early oral PrEP care continuum outcomes among people who inject drugs in Los Angeles and Denver
item.description:
Background: Despite high HIV risk among people who inject drugs (PWID), uptake of pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) remains low. Understanding the role of stigma toward PrEP use among PWID can inform interventions to improve engagement along the PrEP care continuum. We examined associations between PrEP stigma and early PrEP care continuum steps: awareness, willingness to take PrEP, and attempts to access PrEP, among PWID.

Methods: We analyzed data from 243 HIV-negative PWID recruited through community-based and peer outreach efforts in Los Angeles, California, and Denver, Colorado, between April 2021 and June 2023. Participants completed a survey assessing stigma toward PrEP, awareness of PrEP, willingness to take PrEP, and attempts to access PrEP, along with sociodemographic and behavioral factors. This study refers specifically to oral PrEP, the predominant formulation available during the study period. A 10-item PrEP stigma scale assessed attitudes and perceptions toward PrEP use. Stigma items were averaged to create a continuous score (range 0-4). Multivariable logistic regression models estimated associations between PrEP stigma and each PrEP care continuum outcome.

Results: Overall PrEP stigma was relatively low (mean = 1.64, SD = 0.46). Sixty-three percent of participants had heard of PrEP, 46.2% reported willingness to take PrEP, and 5.0% had attempted to access PrEP. PrEP stigma was not associated with awareness of PrEP (aOR = 0.89; 95% CI: 0.46, 1.70). However, higher stigma was significantly associated with lower willingness to take PrEP; each one-point increase in stigma score was associated with 78% lower odds of willingness (aOR = 0.22; 95% CI: 0.10, 0.48). Higher stigma was also associated with lower odds of attempting to access PrEP in unadjusted analyses (OR = 0.15; 95% CI: 0.04, 0.62), but this association was not statistically significant after adjustment (aOR = 0.10; 95% CI: 0.01, 1.05).

Conclusion: Stigma toward PrEP, reflected in negative beliefs and social attitudes about PrEP use, remains an important barrier to willingness to initiate PrEP among PWID. Interventions addressing PrEP-related stigma may improve PrEP engagement and help reduce HIV transmission risk among PWID.

Khezri M, Ivasiy R, Rahman F, Schneider JA, Ompad DC, Friedman SR

item.title: Discrimination and early substance use among racial-ethnically minoritized youth: Self-reports and hair samples
item.description:
Objective: Racial-ethnically minoritized youth are at elevated risk for early substance use (SU; typically defined as occurring before age 15). Research rarely investigates how different forms of discrimination, such as racial-ethnic and weight discrimination, may operate differently by sex. The current study investigated how these two forms of discrimination differentially relate to early SU, assessed subjectively and objectively, among racial-ethnically minoritized boys and girls.

Method: Data were drawn from 571 U.S. racial-ethnically minoritized youth (51% female; Mage=11.75 years old) in the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study, which began in 2016-18. Main exposure variables included racial-ethnic and weight discrimination. Main outcomes included self-reported SU over the past year and hair sample-based SU over the past three months. Sociodemographic and psychosocial covariates that may be related to SU were included. Cross-sectional and longitudinal analyses were conducted, separately by sex assigned at birth.

Results: Logistic regression-based path analysis (accounting for non-independence) revealed sex-specific patterns. Among racial-ethnically minoritized boys, racial-ethnic discrimination was associated with increased likelihood of self-reported early SU concurrently (OR = 1.42; 95%CI = [1.19, 1.71]). Among racial-ethnically minoritized girls, weight discrimination was associated with increased likelihood of hair sample-based early SU concurrently (OR = 3.48; 95% CI = [1.37, 8.83]) and one year later (OR = 3.61; 95% CI = [1.07, 12.23]).

Conclusion: This study underscores the unique influences of racial-ethnic and weight discrimination faced by racial-ethnically minoritized boys and girls, separately. Results highlight the need for programs and practices to address these unique experiences to effectively prevent early SU.

Wang Y, Zhang Y, Yan J, Huang Q, Jelsma E, Zhao Z

item.title: A multi-reward framework to improve translation in alcohol use disorder
item.description:
Background and objectives: Alcohol use disorder (AUD) is a major contributor to global disease burden and a leading cause of preventable death, yet available treatments remain only modestly effective. Although rodent models are widely used to study alcohol-related behaviors and guide pharmacotherapy development, many compounds with strong preclinical efficacy fail clinically. Here, we propose a reward-component framework that separates ethanol intake into four distinct reward components: pre-oral reward, oral reward, post-oral peripheral reward, and post-oral central drug reward. We use this framework to examine whether cross-species differences in the reward components sustaining ethanol intake contribute to translational failure.

Methods: We synthesized behavioral, pharmacological, and neurobiological evidence concerning the contribution of these four reward components to ethanol intake in rodents and humans with AUD, and compared findings across species.

Results: The reward component primarily sustaining high ethanol intake in rodents remains largely unclear, with mixed contributions from oral and post-oral rewards. In contrast, AUD in humans is predominantly sustained by the post-oral central drug reward component, creating a cross-species misalignment in what rewards ethanol intake. Since pharmacotherapies differentially act across multiple components, this cross-species misalignment in reward components involved in ethanol intake between rodents and humans may explain previous translational failures in AUD pharmacotherapy development.

Conclusions: By offering a deeper understanding of past translational failures, this framework provides a basis for developing more valid and predictive preclinical models. Notably, identifying more effective pharmacological interventions will require improved alignment of the reward components controlling ethanol intake in animals and humans with AUD.

Guerrin CGJ, Ahmed SH

item.title: Prenatal care utilization among pregnant women with substance use disorder: A drug-free moms and babies program study
item.description:
Background: Prenatal stimulant and opioid use continue to rise, with disproportionately higher rates observed in rural and socioeconomically disadvantaged populations.

Objective: To examine the association between opioid and stimulant use patterns and prenatal care adequacy among women with substance use disorder (SUD) enrolled in the Drug-Free Moms and Babies (DFMB) program in West Virginia.

Methods: Secondary data analysis of DFMB participants (2018-2022; N = 1264). Opioid and stimulant use were categorized into four mutually exclusive groups. Adequacy of prenatal care was measured using the Kessner Index, categorized as inadequate, intermediate, and adequate.

Results: Pregnant women with SUD who used opioids only [AOR = 2.21 (1.38, 3.57)], stimulants only [AOR = 4.25 (2.01, 8.99)], or both [AOR = 5.42 (2.77, 10.62)] had higher odds of receiving inadequate prenatal care compared with women who did not use these substances. Similarly, women using opioids only [AOR = 2.10 (1.50, 2.94)], stimulants only [AOR = 2.27 (1.18, 4.39)], or both substances [AOR = 2.31 (1.24, 4.33)] were more likely to receive intermediate care.

Discussion: While all substance-use groups demonstrated increased odds of inadequate or intermediate prenatal care, the risk was highest among women using both opioids and stimulants, followed by stimulant use alone.

Conclusions: The study highlights the need to identify and address upstream factors that influence prenatal care engagement among rural pregnant women with SUD, particularly those using opioids and/or stimulants.

Scientific significance: The study identifies the intersection between opioid and stimulant use, prenatal care utilization, and social determinants of health.

Article summary: Opioid and stimulant use during pregnancy was associated with a higher risk of both inadequate and intermediate prenatal care utilization, with the greatest risk observed among those using both substances. Social factors, including social disadvantage, unplanned pregnancy, and larger family size, further contributed to inadequate prenatal care. Together, these findings highlight the need to address upstream social, structural, and substance-related barriers to improve prenatal care engagement and, ultimately, maternal and child health in rural populations.

Umer A, Dawley D, Childers R, Breyel J, Lilly C

item.title: Racial and ethnic disparities in medication for opioid use disorder treatment among medicaid enrollees
item.description:
Background: Racial and ethnic disparities in medications for opioid use disorder (MOUD) access exist, and more research is needed to understand the extent of national and cross-state variation in disparities in Medicaid, the largest payer for MOUD.

Methods: Using Medicaid claims (2017-2022) in 36 states, we conducted a repeated cross-sectional analysis to calculate opioid use disorder (OUD) occurrence and, among those with OUD, MOUD utilization, by enrollee race and ethnicity. Logistic regression models estimated the odds of MOUD receipt (any MOUD; buprenorphine; methadone; naltrexone) by enrollee race and ethnicity. Model 1 adjusted for age, sex, and study year, with year by race and ethnicity interactions; Model 2 additionally adjusted for state fixed effects; Model 3 additionally adjusted for Medicaid expansion status. MOUD receipt was also characterized at the state level.

Results: Compared to White enrollees, adjusted odds ratios (aOR) for receiving any MOUD among OUD-diagnosed enrollees were significantly lower for all other racial and ethnic groups across models. Fully-adjusted results found Black aOR= 0.50; 95% CI= 0.49-0.51; Asian or Pacific Islander aOR= 0.74; 95% CI= 0.70-0.79; Hispanic aOR= 0.92; 95% CI= 0.90-0.93. While MOUD rates grew by 16% per year overall, the time effect was negative for all minoritized racial and ethnic groups, implying worsening disparities. The ratio of treatment receipt comparing Black/White enrollees varied widely across states, ranging from.37 (MS) to.94 (LA).

Conclusions: Results highlight the critical need to identify and address ongoing barriers to MOUD, particularly for minoritized groups, and for further research to understand and address state-level variation in these disparities.

Miles J, Treitler P, Hermida R, Samples H, Gupta S, Duncan A
